qs.q: A preterm neonate born at 30 weeks develops intermittent cessation of breathing lasting longer than 20 seconds accompanied by bradycardia. What is the most likely diagnosis?
qs.e: Apnoea of prematurity is a recognized neurological and respiratory complication in preterm infants. Sepsis presents with systemic signs rather than isolated recurrent apnoea spells.
qs.s: Neonatology 2: Prematurity and Respiratory Disorders: MCQs

qs.q: A newborn delivered after a prolonged obstructed labour shows poor respiratory effort, bradycardia and a 5‑minute Apgar of 2. Which maternal or labour factor most likely contributed to this presentation?
qs.e: Uterine rupture is listed as a fetal and labour factor causing birth asphyxia. Cord prolapse also causes asphyxia but is less directly linked to obstructed labour in this scenario.
qs.s: Neonatology 4: Birth Asphyxia and Neurological Disorders: MCQs

qs.q: A patient with a confirmed cervical spinal cord injury develops profound hypotension associated with bradycardia and warm, vasodilated peripheries. What is the most likely physiological cause of this hemodynamic instability?
o: Paralysis of the parasympathetic outflow from S2 to S4
Complete transection of the anterior spinal artery
Acute internal hemorrhage from associated abdominal trauma
Loss of sympathetic tone from a cord lesion above T6
qs.e: Neurogenic shock is a hemodynamic disturbance caused by loss of sympathetic tone, specifically occurring in cord lesions above T6 due to loss of cardiac sympathetic fibres and splanchnic tone. Hemorrhagic shock typically presents with tachycardia and cold peripheries.
qs.s: Spinal Cord Injury: Assessment, Spinal Shock and Management: MCQs

qs.q: A patient is admitted with neurogenic shock following a spinal cord injury. After adequate fluid resuscitation with isotonic crystalloids, the patient remains hypotensive with bradycardia. What is the most appropriate next step in pharmacological management?
o: Initiate vasopressor therapy with norepinephrine or dopamine
Give furosemide to avoid pulmonary oedema
qs.e: For neurogenic shock, vasopressors (noradrenaline or dopamine) are added after adequate fluid resuscitation to restore vascular tone. Steroids are no longer routinely recommended due to high complication rates.
qs.s: Spinal Cord Injury: Assessment, Spinal Shock and Management: MCQs

qs.q: A preterm neonate presents with temperature instability, apnoea, bradycardia, and a blood-stained gastric residual. Laboratory results show neutropenia and a left shift. How is this clinical picture categorised under Bell's staging?
o: Stage I suspected with systemic signs
Stage IIA mildly ill proven disease
qs.e: Stage I (suspected) features non-specific systemic signs like apnoea, bradycardia, and temperature instability alongside feeding intolerance and occult or mild blood, with normal or mild ileus on X-ray. Proven disease requires definite radiographic signs like pneumatosis.
qs.s: Necrotising Enterocolitis in the Newborn: MCQs

qs.q: A 44-year-old man is admitted with a severe thunderclap headache. A lumbar puncture confirms subarachnoid haemorrhage. During the first 48 hours, he develops frequent premature ventricular complexes and bradycardia. What is the most important initial laboratory parameter to check and correct?
o: Check and correct serum creatinine levels
Check and correct serum potassium levels
Check and correct blood glucose levels
Check and correct serum calcium levels
qs.e: Cardiac arrhythmias occur in up to 90 percent of patients, usually in the first 48 hours, and checking and correcting potassium is an essential step in management. Neurogenic stunned myocardium and ECG changes can also mimic acute coronary syndromes.
qs.s: Subarachnoid Haemorrhage and Intracranial Aneurysms: MCQs

qs.q: A 32‑week preterm twin pregnancy presents with a breech fetus and sudden fetal bradycardia after amniotomy. Which factor most likely contributed to an umbilical cord prolapse?
o: Presence of a short umbilical cord structure
Presence of a breech fetal presentation
Presence of low neonatal birth weight
qs.e: Breech malpresentation is a known risk factor for cord prolapse. Short cord is not listed; long cord is the risk mentioned.
qs.s: Shoulder Dystocia and Umbilical Cord Prolapse: Emergency Management: MCQs

qs.q: During active labour a cord prolapse is identified and the fetal heart rate shows severe bradycardia. Under the classification of urgency, this scenario belongs to which category?
qs.e: Cord prolapse with severe fetal bradycardia threatens immediate fetal life, fitting Category 1. Category 2 involves compromise without immediate threat.
qs.s: Caesarean Section and Perioperative Care: Indications, Technique,: MCQs

ai.title: Bradycardia in Adults
ai.subject: Medicine
ai.summary: Bradycardia is a heart rate below 60 bpm. In low‑resource settings the clinician must identify reversible causes, assess severity, and act quickly when it signals circulatory collapse.

sections.p: A resting heart rate < 60 beats per minute on at least two separate measurements, confirmed by pulse and ECG. Distinguish sinus bradycardia (regular P‑waves) from atrioventricular (AV) block (dropped beats).
b: ECG: rate, rhythm, PR interval, QRS width
Pulse check: regularity, volume, peripheral perfusion

sections.p: Severity is judged by symptoms and hemodynamics rather than a numeric stage.
b: Asymptomatic, HR 50‑59 bpm – mild
Symptomatic (dizziness, syncope, fatigue) – moderate
Hypotension, altered mental status, shock – severe/urgent

sections.p: Group causes by location (sinus node, AV node, systemic). In East African hospitals the common reversible triggers dominate.
b: Medication: beta‑blockers, non‑DHP calcium‑channel blockers, digoxin, anti‑arrhythmics, clonidine
Infections: severe malaria, sepsis, HIV‑related opportunistic infections, TB meningitis
Electrolyte disturbance: hyperkalemia, severe hypoxia
Endocrine: hypothyroidism, adrenal insufficiency
Ischemia: inferior myocardial infarction, right coronary artery disease
Structural: rheumatic heart disease with conduction system involvement, congenital AV block

sections.p: Patients may be asymptomatic, or report fatigue, light‑headedness, presyncope, or syncope. In severe cases they appear pale, cool, with low blood pressure and altered consciousness.
b: Slow, regular pulse
Reduced cardiac output signs: hypotension, cold extremities
Neurologic: dizziness, confusion, seizures if cerebral hypoperfusion

sections.p: Select tests that answer a specific clinical question; if a test is unavailable, use bedside alternatives.

t.b: What is the rhythm and site of block? – Confirms sinus vs. AV block; guides need for pacing
Are electrolyte abnormalities contributing? – Hyper‑K+ > 5.5 mmol/L suggests block; treat accordingly
Is hypothyroidism present? – Elevated TSH with low T4 supports endocrine cause
Is a bradycardic drug being taken? – Identifies reversible iatrogenic cause
Is there pericardial effusion or tamponade? – Echo shows effusion; treat emergently

t.a: If ECG unavailable: manual pulse check and blood pressure
t.b: Is the patient hemodynamically stable? – Low BP with slow pulse mandates urgent transfer

sections.p: Bradycardia can progress to cardiac arrest if perfusion falls.
b: Systolic BP < 90 mmHg with HR < 50 bpm
Syncope or presyncope repeatedly
Signs of shock: cold, clammy skin, altered mental status
New AV block progressing to complete block

sections.p: Treat the underlying cause first; provide temporary support while arranging definitive therapy.
b: Stop or reduce bradycardic drugs; switch to alternative antihypertensives if needed
Correct electrolytes: give calcium gluconate for hyper‑K+, IV magnesium for torsades risk
Treat hypothyroidism with levothyroxine (once diagnosis confirmed)
If ischemic: give aspirin, oxygen, and arrange reperfusion if MI suspected
Temporary pacing: transcutaneous pacing for unstable patients; consider transvenous pacing if prolonged

sections.p: After acute stabilization, arrange outpatient review to address chronic causes and monitor for recurrence.
b: Repeat ECG after drug withdrawal or electrolyte correction
Thyroid panel follow‑up in 6‑8 weeks if abnormal
Educate patient on medication side‑effects and when to seek care
Vaccination and malaria prophylaxis for high‑risk patients

sections.p: Conditions that mimic a slow pulse but have different management.
b: Sinus pause vs. atrial fibrillation with slow ventricular response
Hypotension without bradycardia (e.g., septic shock)
Heart block vs. sick sinus syndrome

sections.p: Be aware of false‑negative or misleading findings.
b: ECG may show normal rate if patient is anxious; repeat after rest
Serum potassium can be spuriously low in severe acidosis – interpret with ABG
Pulse oximetry may read normal SpO₂ despite low cardiac output; assess perfusion clinically

whenToSeekHelp: Systolic BP < 90 mmHg with HR < 50 bpm
Chest pain with bradycardia suggesting inferior MI

faq.q: Is a heart rate of 58 bpm always abnormal?
faq.a: No; athletes and well‑conditioned individuals may have resting rates 50‑60 bpm without symptoms.
Severe malaria can lead to high‑output failure and electrolyte shifts that precipitate bradycardia.
Avoid in patients with known 2nd‑degree type II or complete AV block unless a temporary pacemaker is ready.

exam: A 45‑year‑old farmer on propranolol presents with dizziness and HR 48 bpm – what is your immediate step? — Review medication, stop propranolol, assess hemodynamics, give atropine if unstable.
How does an inferior myocardial infarction produce bradycardia? — Explain Bezold‑Jarisch reflex and SA/AV node ischemia from right coronary artery involvement.

A patient with HIV on cotrimoxazole develops HR 55 bpm and hyperkalemia; what is the pathophysiology and treatment? — Drug‑induced potassium retention causing conduction delay; stop offending drug, give calcium gluconate, consider dialysis if severe.
What ECG features differentiate sinus bradycardia from second‑degree AV block type I? — Sinus bradycardia shows normal PR interval; Mobitz I shows progressive PR prolongation then dropped beat.
When is temporary pacing indicated in bradycardia? — Unstable hemodynamics (hypotension, syncope) despite atropine, or high‑grade AV block.
Why is digoxin toxicity a concern in bradycardia and how is it identified? — Causes AV block; look for visual disturbances, hyperkalemia, and characteristic ‘scooped’ ST segments on ECG.

In a low‑resource clinic without ECG, how would you assess a patient with suspected bradyarrhythmia? — Measure pulse, blood pressure, assess symptoms, review meds, and perform bedside cardiac exam for murmurs or pericardial rub.
What preventive measures reduce recurrent bradycardia in patients with hypothyroidism? — Adequate levothyroxine replacement, regular TSH monitoring, and avoidance of bradycardic drugs.

sections.h: Bedside: history and how to examine
sections.p: Focused history and systematic exam reveal the cause, severity and hemodynamic impact of bradycardia, especially where investigations are limited.
b: Onset: sudden vs gradual; relation to drug changes, infection, trauma or myocardial infarction
Associated symptoms: dizziness, syncope, fatigue, chest pain, dyspnoea, fever, recent malaria or sepsis
Medication review: beta‑blockers, non‑DHP calcium‑channel blockers, digoxin, clonidine, anti‑arrhythmics, herbal remedies
Recent electrolyte disturbances: vomiting, diarrhoea, dialysis, potassium‑sparing diuretics
Endocrine history: hypothyroidism, adrenal insufficiency, pregnancy, diabetes control
HIV/TB status, recent opportunistic infection or antiretroviral change
Family history of congenital conduction disease or rheumatic fever

t.b: Is the rate <60 bpm? Is it regular? Volume and peripheral perfusion indicate output; a weak, thready pulse suggests low stroke volume – cannot determine block level
Systolic <90 mmHg with bradycardia defines hemodynamic instability – does not differentiate sinus vs AV block
Elevated JVP with bradycardia may point to right‑sided MI or tamponade – bedside cannot quantify exact pressure
Bradycardic rhythm may reveal murmurs of ischemia or prosthetic valve dysfunction – cannot identify precise conduction defect
Confusion or seizures suggest cerebral hypoperfusion – does not specify arrhythmia cause

sections.h: Investigations and how to read them
sections.p: Select tests that answer a specific clinical question; use bedside alternatives when equipment is lacking.
b: ECG – confirms rate, rhythm, PR interval, QRS width; sinus bradycardia shows P‑wave before each QRS, PR 120‑200 ms; second‑degree AV block type I shows progressive PR prolongation then dropped beat
Serum electrolytes – potassium >6.0 mmol/L may cause bradycardia; calcium <1.9 mmol/L can prolong PR; magnesium <0.7 mmol/L worsens AV block
Thyroid function – TSH >10 mIU/L supports hypothyroidism as reversible cause
Cardiac enzymes – troponin rise with inferior MI suggests vagal‑mediated sinus node suppression
Chest X‑ray – enlarged cardiac silhouette or pulmonary congestion may indicate structural disease
Echocardiography – assesses wall motion, valve disease, pericardial effusion; low EF explains low output bradycardia
Holter or event monitor – quantifies intermittent pauses when ECG unavailable

t.b: Answers: rhythm origin, block level, drug effect. Look for sinus P‑waves, PR interval, dropped QRS. If no ECG, use pulse‑ox waveform to estimate regularity
>6.0 mmol/L suggests hyperkalaemia‑induced bradycardia; >9.0 mmol/L may show sine‑wave pattern – if lab unavailable, use bedside potassium dipstick
<1.9 mmol/L (ionized <1.1 mmol/L) may prolong PR; correct before attributing block to intrinsic disease
>10 mIU/L indicates hypothyroidism; treat to improve rate – normal TSH does not exclude other causes
Elevated with inferior MI; supports vagal sinus node suppression – normal troponin makes ischemia less likely

sections.p: Classification integrates heart rate, symptoms, hemodynamics and underlying mechanism.
b: Bradycardia defined as resting HR <60 bpm confirmed by pulse and ECG
Symptomatic mild: HR 50‑59 bpm with dizziness or fatigue but stable BP
Moderate: HR <50 bpm with presyncope, syncope or mild hypotension (SBP 90‑100 mmHg)
Severe/urgent: HR <50 bpm with SBP <90 mmHg, altered mental status, shock or high‑grade AV block
Mechanistic staging: sinus node dysfunction, AV nodal block (type I, type II, complete), drug‑induced, metabolic, ischemic, structural

sections.p: Conditions that mimic bradycardia must be differentiated by history, exam and targeted tests.

t.a: Hypotension with low pulse pressure from hypovolemia
t.b: History of fluid loss, dry mucous membranes; BP low with narrow pulse pressure; ECG shows normal rate – treat with fluids, not pacing
Cold intolerance, dry skin, delayed reflexes; TSH markedly raised; ECG may show sinus bradycardia but correction of thyroid hormone improves rate
History of overdose, bronchospasm, miosis; ECG shows sinus bradycardia; treat with glucagon and atropine before pacing
Recent neuraxial block, loss of sympathetic tone; bradycardia with hypotension, warm flushed skin; resolves as block wears off – no intrinsic conduction disease

sections.p: A structured ladder guides immediate stabilisation, reversible‑cause treatment, and definitive therapy while continuously reassessing haemodynamics and rhythm.
b: 1. Assess airway, breathing, circulation; place patient supine, give high‑flow oxygen, attach cardiac monitor and pulse oximeter.

3. Treat reversible causes: stop offending drugs (beta‑blockers, non‑DHP CCBs, digoxin), correct electrolyte abnormalities (hyper‑/hypokalaemia, severe hypocalcaemia <1.9 mmol/L), treat hypoxia, give IV glucose for severe hypothyroidism, treat infection with appropriate antibiotics.
4. If no response to atropine and high‑grade AV block or unstable sinus bradycardia persists, prepare transcutaneous pacing; consider dopamine or epinephrine only after pacing attempts fail.

5. Initiate disease‑specific definitive therapy: permanent pacemaker for symptomatic sick‑sinus syndrome or persistent second‑degree type II/complete AV block; treat myocardial infarction with reperfusion; manage hypothyroidism with levothyroxine.
6. Continuous monitoring: telemetry for rhythm changes, invasive blood pressure if available, urine output, mental status; repeat ECG after each intervention.
7. Escalate to higher‑level care or cardiology when pacing required, drug toxicity suspected, or haemodynamics do not improve within 15 minutes of initial measures.

sections.h: Drug effects and what to do
sections.p: Understanding adverse actions and interactions prevents iatrogenic worsening of bradycardia.
b: Atropine: may cause tachycardia, dry mouth, urinary retention; if tachyarrhythmia develops, stop further doses.
Beta‑blockers: can mask hypoglycaemia and worsen asthma; if bradycardia persists, discontinue and consider glucagon for severe hypoglycaemia.
Non‑DHP calcium‑channel blockers (verapamil, diltiazem): depress AV node; avoid in sick‑sinus syndrome; treat toxicity with calcium gluconate and high‑dose insulin‑glucose.
Digoxin: causes AV block, nausea, visual disturbances; check serum level; if toxic, give digoxin‑specific Fab fragments; avoid concurrent quinidine or macrolides.
Clonidine: central α2‑agonist; abrupt withdrawal can precipitate rebound hypertension; treat bradycardia with atropine and consider tapering.
Potassium‑sparing diuretics (spironolactone, trimethoprim‑sulfamethoxazole): raise serum K; if K >6.0 mmol/L, give calcium gluconate, insulin‑glucose, and consider dialysis.

sections.p: Recognise early signs of decompensation to trigger higher‑level interventions.
b: Progressive hypotension (SBP <90 mmHg) despite atropine → start transcutaneous pacing.
Altered mental status or seizures → consider cerebral hypoperfusion; secure airway, give oxygen, treat underlying rhythm.
Chest pain or new ST‑segment changes → suspect myocardial ischaemia; urgent ECG, analgesia, and reperfusion pathway.
Signs of shock (cold, clammy skin, oliguria) with bradycardia → initiate fluid bolus, vasopressor (norepinephrine) after pacing if needed.
Development of high‑grade AV block on serial ECGs → arrange urgent cardiology review for permanent pacemaker.

sections.p: Co‑morbidities and local factors modify presentation, investigations and therapy.
b: HIV infection: opportunistic CNS infections and ART (e.g., protease inhibitors) can cause bradycardia; check CD4, treat infection, review ART for QT‑prolonging agents.
Tuberculosis: meningitis or pericardial involvement may depress sinus node; start anti‑TB therapy, monitor electrolytes, avoid rifampicin‑induced hepatic dysfunction affecting drug metabolism.
Malnutrition: low magnesium and calcium predispose to conduction delay; replace electrolytes before giving chronotropic drugs.
Pregnancy: physiological HR increase masks bradycardia; avoid teratogenic drugs (e.g., amiodarone); use atropine and pacing if needed.
Diabetes: autonomic neuropathy may blunt tachycardic response; monitor glucose, avoid beta‑blockers if severe hypoglycaemia risk.
Herbal remedies (e.g., hawthorn, yohimbine): may interact with digoxin or beta‑blockers; obtain thorough medication history.
Alcohol excess: can cause electrolyte loss and direct myocardial depression; correct K/Mg, counsel abstinence.
Renal failure: reduces clearance of digoxin and potassium‑sparing agents; use lower‑dose digoxin, monitor K closely.
Liver failure: impairs metabolism of beta‑blockers and CCBs; dose‑adjust or avoid.

sections.p: Tailor assessment and therapy to physiological differences and resource constraints.
b: Pregnancy: avoid drugs that cross placenta with fetal toxicity; prioritize non‑pharmacologic measures, use atropine, and consider temporary pacing if haemodynamically unstable.
Elderly: higher prevalence of sick‑sinus syndrome and polypharmacy; review all rate‑slowing drugs, start with low‑dose atropine, monitor for hypotension.
People with HIV: drug‑drug interactions with protease inhibitors; monitor digoxin levels, adjust doses of beta‑blockers, treat opportunistic infections promptly.
Low‑resource settings: when ECG unavailable, rely on pulse palpation, blood pressure, and bedside capillary refill; use clinical algorithms to decide on atropine vs. referral for pacing.

facts: Bradycardia: resting heart rate <60 bpm confirmed by pulse and ECG.
Sinus bradycardia: regular rhythm, normal P‑wave morphology, PR 120‑200 ms.
Second‑degree AV block type I (Wenckebach): progressive PR prolongation, dropped beat, grouped beating.
Temporary transcutaneous pacing is indicated if no response to atropine and high‑grade AV block persists.
Digoxin toxicity typically presents with heart rate <60 bpm, nausea, visual disturbances, and scooped ST segments.
Hyperkalemia >6.0 mmol/L produces peaked T waves; sine wave pattern appears >9.0 mmol/L.
Calcium <1.9 mmol/L (ionized <1.1 mmol/L) may prolong PR interval.
Hypothyroidism can cause bradycardia; free T4 low, TSH elevated.
Beta‑blocker overdose: treat with glucagon after atropine if needed.

vivas.q: Define bradycardia and how you confirm it at the bedside.
vivas.a: Heart rate <60 bpm confirmed by palpating a regular pulse and verifying on a 12‑lead ECG for rate, rhythm and PR interval.

vivas.q: What bedside steps do you take to assess a patient with suspected bradyarrhythmia when ECG is unavailable?
vivas.a: Palpate radial pulse, count beats for 60 seconds, assess regularity, volume, capillary refill, blood pressure, and look for symptoms of low output.

vivas.q: How does an inferior myocardial infarction cause bradycardia?
vivas.a: Ischemia of the right coronary artery impairs the sinus node and vagal afferents, producing sinus bradycardia or AV nodal block.

vivas.q: Explain the ECG differences between sinus bradycardia and second‑degree AV block type I.
vivas.a: Sinus bradycardia shows constant PR; Wenckebach shows progressive PR prolongation then a dropped QRS after a variable number of beats.

vivas.q: When is temporary pacing indicated in bradycardia?
vivas.a: If symptomatic bradycardia persists after atropine and the patient has high‑grade AV block or unstable hemodynamics.

vivas.q: Why is digoxin toxicity a concern in bradycardia and how is it identified?
vivas.a: Toxic levels depress AV nodal conduction; look for HR <60 bpm, nausea, visual halos, and ECG changes such as scooped ST segments or AV block.

vivas.q: What are the key history questions for bradycardia in a low‑resource setting?
vivas.a: Ask about medication use (beta‑blockers, calcium‑channel blockers, digoxin), recent infections, hypothyroid symptoms, chest pain, syncope, and exposure to toxins.

vivas.q: List the physical signs that suggest low cardiac output due to bradycardia.
vivas.a: Hypotension, cool clammy extremities, delayed capillary refill, altered mental status, and reduced urine output.

vivas.q: Which investigations answer the question ‘Is this sinus bradycardia or AV block?’
vivas.a: 12‑lead ECG (rate, rhythm, PR interval, QRS width) and, if unavailable, a portable monitor or telemetry strip.

vivas.q: How do you manage bradycardia caused by severe hypothyroidism?
vivas.a: Start levothyroxine replacement; monitor heart rate and give atropine if symptomatic until thyroid hormone takes effect.

vivas.q: A preterm neonate born at 30 weeks develops intermittent cessation of breathing >20 s with bradycardia. What is the most likely diagnosis?
A newborn after prolonged obstructed labour shows poor effort, bradycardia, Apgar 2 at 5 min. Which maternal/labour factor most likely contributed?
vivas.a: Uterine rupture or severe fetal hypoxia from prolonged compression.

vivas.q: A patient with cervical spinal cord injury develops profound hypotension, bradycardia, warm vasodilated peripheries. What is the physiological cause?
vivas.a: Neurogenic shock from loss of sympathetic tone and unopposed vagal activity.

vivas.q: After fluid resuscitation for neurogenic shock, the patient remains hypotensive with bradycardia. What is the most appropriate next step?
vivas.a: Administer IV atropine; if no response, start low‑dose dopamine or norepinephrine to support heart rate and vascular tone.

vivas.q: A preterm neonate presents with temperature instability, apnoea, bradycardia, blood‑stained gastric residual, neutropenia and left shift. How is this categorized under Bell’s staging?
vivas.a: Stage II (probable NEC) – systemic signs with intestinal involvement.

vivas.q: A 44‑year‑old with subarachnoid haemorrhage develops frequent PVCs and bradycardia in the first 48 h. What explains this pattern?
vivas.a: Cerebral vagal stimulation from increased intracranial pressure causing reflex bradycardia and ventricular ectopy.

vivas.q: A 32‑week preterm twin pregnancy with breech fetus has sudden fetal bradycardia after amniotomy. Which factor most likely caused umbilical cord prolapse?
vivas.a: Long umbilical cord with insufficient amniotic fluid allowing cord descent after membrane rupture.

vivas.q: During active labour a cord prolapse is identified and fetal heart rate shows severe bradycardia. Under the classification of urgency, which category does this scenario belong to?
vivas.a: Category 1 – immediate threat to fetal life requiring emergency delivery.

mcqs.q: A patient on digoxin presents with HR 52 bpm, nausea, and visual halos. Which ECG finding supports digoxin toxicity?
mcqs.e: Digoxin causes characteristic down‑sloping (scooped) ST segment depression.

mcqs.q: In a low‑resource clinic without ECG, which sign most reliably indicates a high‑grade AV block?
o: Very slow regular pulse with occasional missed beats
mcqs.e: A regular slow pulse with occasional dropped beats suggests AV block not sinus bradycardia.

mcqs.q: Which of the following is NOT a reversible cause of bradycardia in East African hospitals?
o: Rheumatic heart disease with conduction involvement
mcqs.e: Congenital complete heart block is not reversible.

mcqs.q: A patient with neurogenic shock remains bradycardic after fluids. Which drug is most appropriate next?
mcqs.e: Atropine directly increases heart rate; catecholamines are second line.

cases.v: A 28‑year‑old male farmer on propranolol for hypertension presents with dizziness, fatigue, HR 48 bpm, BP 110/70 mmHg, no chest pain.

qs.q: Which investigation confirms the type of bradyarrhythmia?
qs.a: 12‑lead ECG to assess rhythm, PR interval and QRS morphology.
Review and adjust antihypertensive regimen, avoid non‑selective beta‑blockers if not needed, and monitor heart rate regularly.

cases.v: A 3‑month‑old preterm infant (30 weeks gestation) in a rural clinic develops apnoea episodes lasting 25 seconds with HR dropping to 80 bpm, oxygen saturation 85%. No infection signs.

qs.q: What is the most likely diagnosis?

qs.a: Gentle tactile stimulation; if ineffective, provide CPAP or brief positive pressure ventilation.

qs.q: What medication can reduce episodes if they persist?
qs.a: Caffeine citrate, if available; otherwise, monitor and ensure adequate thermal regulation.

mistakes: Confusing sinus bradycardia with Wenckebach AV block; remember PR progression in Wenckebach.
Using dopamine or epinephrine before atropine for symptomatic bradycardia.
Assuming digoxin toxicity only when serum level >2 ng/mL; clinical signs are more reliable.
Neglecting to assess medication history, especially beta‑blockers and calcium‑channel blockers.
Failing to consider hypothyroidism as a reversible cause of bradycardia.
Attempting permanent pacing without first correcting reversible metabolic disturbances.
Misinterpreting a regular slow pulse as benign when it may represent high‑grade AV block.
